questions.question: Two candidates give identical answers, but one says 'Me and him did it.' Both are understood perfectly. Why does grammar still decide who gets the job?
questions.solution: Because grammar is a SOCIAL SIGNAL, not just a clarity tool. Listeners unconsciously read non-standard forms as evidence about education, attention to detail and professionalism — fair or not. 'Him and I did it' vs 'Me and him did it' carry identical information but opposite prestige. English grammar rules persist because institutions reward them: exams, interviews and publications filter on form as a proxy for care. Mastering grammar buys credibility; the meaning was never the only message.

questions.question: Student A memorises 50 new words weekly but can't use them; Student B learns 10 weekly in full sentences and outscores A. What is wrong with word-list learning, neurologically?
questions.solution: Memory stores words as NETWORKS, not lists — a word survives if linked to contexts, images, collocations and emotions. Isolated words (apple = स्याउ) form single fragile links that decay within days. Sentence-learned words build multiple retrieval paths (situation, grammar pattern, feeling), so each encounter strengthens a web, not a thread. Breadth without depth is sand: impressive weekly, gone monthly. Learn fewer words with richer connections — retrieval beats storage.

questions.concept: Why authors never say it directly
questions.question: A poet writes 'the fog comes on little cat feet' instead of 'fog arrived quietly.' If clarity is a virtue, why does literature deliberately AVOID saying things plainly?
questions.solution: Because literature's job is EXPERIENCE transfer, not information transfer. 'Quietly' reports a fact; cat-feet MAKE you feel stealth, softness, watchfulness — the metaphor recruits your senses and memory, so the fog lands in your body, not just your notes. Direct statement is efficient for manuals; indirection is powerful for meaning. Analysis asks: what work does this image do that plain words couldn't? That work IS the literature.

questions.question: In group discussions, the student who speaks MOST usually scores LOWEST. What are evaluators actually rewarding, and how does listening earn marks?
questions.solution: Evaluators reward BUILDING on others: referencing a previous point ('As Sita argued…'), synthesising ('Both views agree that…'), and inviting quieter members in. Dominating signals poor teamwork — the very skill GDs test. Listening earns marks three ways: better content (you respond to what was actually said), visible courtesy (nodding, noting), and strategic timing (a single well-placed summary outweighs ten interruptions). Talk less, connect more: discussion is a team sport scored on assists, not goals.

questions.question: Two students spend one hour each: A writes one perfect draft slowly; B writes a fast messy draft then revises twice. B's essay scores far higher on the same knowledge. What does revision add that careful first-drafting cannot?
questions.solution: Distance. First drafts serve the writer's thinking (getting ideas OUT); revision serves the READER (structure, cuts, clarity). You cannot simultaneously generate ideas and judge them — the brain modes conflict, so A's 'careful' draft is really just slow generation with no quality pass. B's second draft deletes dead weight, reorders for logic, and sharpens sentences — improvements invisible while generating. Professional writers draft fast and edit ruthlessly: writing is thinking, editing is communicating.
